chapter_theme: Evening, once a friend, returns as an executioner. The woman speaks to the hour, quarrels with it and maps her sickness through the day, ending on the man whose nature, she says, has become wealth itself.
structure_note: All ten are the woman's. Parimelazhagar has her addressing evening itself (1221-1222), answering her friend (1223-1227), and describing its signs and effects (1228-1230). The chapter's main contrast is between evening as it was when they were together and evening as it is now.

1221.reading: The woman tells the hour, with a bitter blessing, that it isn't evening at all but வேலை, which eats the life of those once wed.

positions.position: வேலை is a time word, the hour of ending, and he mentions but sets aside others who take it as 'you've become a spear'.
The word is வேல் plus ஐ: you have become a spear that eats life. He adds evening is hot, so it's not really evening.
Also a spear that drinks life, with the blessing made explicit.
positions.quote: உயிரைக் குடிக்கும் வேலாக இருப்பதற்காக உனக்கோர் வாழ்த்து!

1222.reading: The woman says to the bewildered evening, may you live, you look sad-eyed; is your partner as hard-eyed as mine?
1222.nuance: The tender moment of the chapter: she stops fighting the hour and sees it as a fellow sufferer. Parimelazhagar explains that the pale evening's fading of light is what suggests its grief, and says she has put her own inner state onto it. The word மருள் means both the mixing of day and night and being confused.

1223.reading: The woman says that evening, which comes with chill and pale, now comes with revulsion budding and sorrow growing.
1223.nuance: Parimelazhagar glosses துனி strongly, as disgust with living. Evening used to tremble and pale before her when she was happy; now she trembles before it. Manakkudavar keeps the reversal smaller, with today's evening following yesterday's.

1224.reading: The woman says that when her lover is absent, evening comes like enemies coming to a killing ground.
1224.nuance: ஏதிலர் is the word she has been using of the town and of the man's accusers; Parimelazhagar glosses it here as 'those with no grace at all', executioners. That evening was once her friend is part of the pain.

1225.reading: The woman asks what good she has done to morning and what enmity she has shown to evening.
1225.nuance: It is framed as a legal puzzle about reward and punishment. Both commentators note a hidden reversal: morning used to be the hated hour, when they feared his leaving, and now it's the shore at the end of the flood of night. Evening made the opposite change.

1226.reading: The woman says she didn't know that evening brings sickness, while he who wed her had not yet left.
1226.nuance: It answers the most painful question: why did you consent? Parimelazhagar spells out that she would have refused had she known this. So 1181's self-accusation gets its answer: she agreed in ignorance.

1227.reading: The woman says this sickness buds in the morning, ripens through the day and opens in the evening.
1227.nuance: A flower is made a sickness, in a lovely, cruel inversion. Parimelazhagar's reasons are as vivid as the verse: at morning she is still comforted by a dream, by day memory thins, and at evening she watches creatures and people returning to their mates.

1228.reading: The woman says the herdsman's flute is a messenger for the burning evening and a weapon that kills.
1228.nuance: The one sound in the chapter, pastoral and sweet in itself. Parimelazhagar reads it as a change from 'pleasant before' to deadly now. Evening has its own envoy and arms, like a king making war.

1229.reading: The woman says that when evening spreads, bewildering the mind, the whole town is bewildered and suffers.
1229.nuance: Parimelazhagar's gloss is missing in this source, but his note says the unstated thought is 'I shall die', and he treats evening as Death, implying that the town grieves for her. He adds that others read it as her own mind reeling, and with so little of his comment left, I can't say which he preferred in full.

1230.reading: The woman says that thinking of the one whose nature is wealth, in this confused evening, her life that wouldn't die is dying.
1230.nuance: The wordplay does much of the work: பொருள்மாலை, 'wealth-natured', against மருள்மாலை, 'confused evening', and மாயும் against மாயா. For Parimelazhagar, he has broken his word to keep to wealth, so he has lost his nature to it. Manakkudavar says she takes him to have neither love nor virtue.

links.note: 759 tells the reader bluntly to make wealth, for nothing cuts an enemy's pride so sharply. 1230 gives the cost of that advice from where it falls: a man whose nature has become wealth, and a woman who is dying of it. The separate books don't reconcile the claims.

In 1135 the man complains of evening's anguish, and Parimelazhagar says love flowers at evening. 1227 makes that a full image in the woman's voice. Evening afflicts both, so longing's timetable isn't gendered, though only his has the palmyra horse.

1152 is the moment when even union was spoiled by the fear of parting, and on the commentators' reading of 1225 it was morning that brought this fear. Now that the feared thing has happened, morning is innocent. Fear has its own hours.

source_issues: 1229: Parimelazhagar's entry is truncated. It starts at மாலை படர்தரும் போழ்து, so his headnote and main gloss are missing.
1230: Pope's prose is cut off mid-sentence ('at the thought of him who').
1222: Parimelazhagar's entry has மருள் வாலை - மயங்கிய மாலாய், typos for மாலை and மாலாய்/மாலையே.
1226: Parimelazhagar's note has a closing parenthesis with no opening one, which suggests that a word விளக்கம் has been lost.
